core: Inventory of the solar system: the Sun, eight planets, five officially named dwarf planets, hundreds of moons, and thousands of asteroids and comets

Layout: four inner terrestrial planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars); four outer giant planets (Jupiter and Saturn as gas giants, Uranus and Neptune as ice giants); the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter; the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune; the Oort Cloud as the distant spherical shell

Nebular theory of formation: the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of interstellar gas and dust; the collapse produced a spinning disk (the solar nebula), the Sun formed at the center, and the planets assembled from clumping material in the disk
Scale: the astronomical unit (AU) as the Earth-Sun distance; planet distances in AU from 0.39 (Mercury) to 30.06 (Neptune); the solar system is mostly empty space
Why the solar system matters as context for Earth
supporting: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's mass (99.80 percent per OpenStax Table 7.1)
All eight planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in roughly the same plane, with nearly circular orbits

Asteroids are rocky remnants concentrated between Mars and Jupiter that never came together into a planet; comets are icy remnants stored in the cold outer regions; dwarf planets include Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea, and Makemake
The solar system orbits the Milky Way's center at about 515,000 mph (828,000 kph), completing one orbit roughly every 230 million years
Earth is so far the only place where life has been found in the solar system
Compositional gradient: only rocky material withstood the young Sun's heat in the inner system; ice, liquid, and gas settled in the outer regions

claims.claim: The solar system includes the Sun, eight planets, five officially named dwarf planets, hundreds of moons, and thousands of asteroids and comets.
An astronomical unit (AU) is the distance from the Sun to Earth, about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers); it is the standard measuring stick for distances within the solar system.

The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are terrestrial planets: small worlds with solid, rocky surfaces. The four outer planets are giants: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, and Uranus and Neptune are ice giants, made of materials that settled in the cooler outer regions.
The asteroid belt occupies the space mostly between Mars and Jupiter; asteroids are rocky remnants of the early solar system that never quite came together into a planet.

Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies almost all smaller than dwarf planet Pluto; farther out, the Oort Cloud is a spherical shell of icy debris extending from about 5,000 to 100,000 AU that has never been directly observed but is predicted from mathematical models and observations of comets.
The Sun contains more than 99 percent of the solar system's mass; OpenStax Astronomy 2e lists the Sun's share as 99.80 percent, with Jupiter holding most of the remainder.

Distances of the planets from the Sun range from 0.39 AU (Mercury) to 30.06 AU (Neptune): Venus 0.72, Earth 1.00, Mars 1.52, Jupiter 5.20, Saturn 9.54, Uranus 19.18. At a scale of one billion to one, Earth sits 150 meters from the Sun and Neptune about 30 city blocks away, showing that the solar system is mostly empty space.

According to the nebular theory, the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a dense cloud of interstellar gas and dust; the cloud collapsed and spun into a disk (the solar nebula), the Sun formed at the center, and planets grew as material in the disk clumped together.

Evidence for the nebular theory includes the planets' shared orbital plane and direction (matching the Sun's spin, as a collapsing spinning cloud would produce) and the observation of flattened disks of gas and dust around young stars elsewhere.

The solar system orbits the center of the Milky Way galaxy at about 515,000 mph (828,000 kph), completing one orbit roughly every 230 million years; so far, Earth is the only place in the solar system where life has been found.

positions: NASA: the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: the objects formed together with the Sun about 4.5 billion years ago
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The values differ only by rounding of the same estimate; the lesson states 'about 4.6 billion years ago' attributed to NASA and notes the estimate is roughly 4.5-4.6 billion years.

positions: NASA: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants

OpenStax Astronomy 2e: all four are jovian (giant) planets, with Jupiter and Saturn the hydrogen-helium 'gas' pair and Uranus and Neptune smaller with proportionally smaller hydrogen-helium atmospheres
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No factual conflict; the lesson follows NASA's gas-giant/ice-giant naming and notes OpenStax groups all four as giant planets.

positions: NASA facts page: about 1.4 million asteroids and about 4,000 comets are in the solar system
These are catalogued estimates; the discovery count grows as surveys improve
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the counts as approximate ('about') and attributes them to NASA, without implying a complete inventory.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The Sun's share of the solar system's mass
positions: NASA: the Sun amassed more than 99% of the available matter
OpenStax Table 7.1: the Sun is 99.80% of the solar system's mass
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Compatible; the lesson says 'more than 99 percent' and cites the 99.80 percent figure as OpenStax's.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate ('Solar System is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.') contained no factual claims and was replaced entirely with verified content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft boilerplate (no factual content) with a sourced lesson: inventory, layout, nebular theory, AU scale, and Earth context.

All quantitative figures (planet count, dwarf-planet count, AU definition, planet distances in AU, scale-model distances, Sun mass share, Oort Cloud extent) were verified against the cited NASA and OpenStax pages and checked arithmetically in python3 on 2026-08-21.
The solar system is presented as mostly empty space via the OpenStax one-billion-to-one scale model rather than as a crowded region.
Member classes (Sun, terrestrial planets, gas giants, moons, asteroids and comets) are named and pointed to their sibling topics rather than taught in depth.

sourceRecords.title: Solar System Overview
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200; no archive copy needed). Tier A. Supports: the inventory (Sun, eight planets, five officially named dwarf planets, hundreds of moons, thousands of asteroids and comets); the layout (terrestrial planets Mercury-Venus-Earth-Mars; gas giants Jupiter and Saturn; ice giants Uranus and Neptune; Kuiper Belt as a ring of icy bodies past Neptune; Oort Cloud as a never-directly-observed spherical shell extending from about 5,000 to 100,000 AU); the AU definition (about 93 million miles / 150 million kilometers); and the nebular formation account (about 4.6 billion years ago, collapsing dense cloud, spinning solar-nebula disk, Sun born at center amassing more than 99% of the matter, asteroid belt as leftover material that never formed a planet). Also supports the ~230-million-year galactic orbit and the Milky Way location. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, 7.1 Overview of Our Planetary System
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200; no archive copy needed). Tier B. Supports: the Sun as 99.80% of the solar system's mass; all eight planets orbiting the Sun in the same direction in approximately the same plane; inner terrestrial planets (small, rock and metal, solid surfaces) versus jovian/giant planets (much larger, lighter ices, liquids, and gases); the planet distance table in AU (Mercury 0.39, Venus 0.72, Earth 1.00, Mars 1.52, Jupiter 5.20, Saturn 9.54, Uranus 19.18, Neptune 30.06); asteroids as rocky bodies mostly between Mars and Jupiter that are remnants of the pre-planet population; comets as icy remnants stored in the cold outer regions; dwarf planets (Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake); more than 210 known moons with only Mercury and Venus moonless; and the 1:1,000,000,000 scale model (Sun about 1.5 m, Earth a grape at 150 m, Jupiter ~5 blocks, Neptune ~30 blocks, nearest stars tens of thousands of kilometers away) demonstrating that the solar system is mostly empty space. Facts synthesized into original prose; no table or wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, 7.2 Composition and Structure of Planets
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200; no archive copy needed). Tier B. Supports the two kinds of planets: rocky terrestrial planets made of silicates and metals versus gas-rich giant planets; Jupiter and Saturn dominated by hydrogen and helium with compressed interiors and rock, metal, and ice cores; Uranus and Neptune smaller with proportionally smaller hydrogen-helium atmospheres and hydrogen-dominated chemistry; water ice abundant throughout the outer solar system. Used to support the inner/outer compositional split in the layout section. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, 7.4 Origin of the Solar System
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200; no archive copy needed). Tier B. Supports the nebular model as the accepted explanation: the planets' shared orbital plane and direction plus the Sun's matching spin interpreted as evidence that the Sun and planets formed together from a spinning cloud of gas and dust (the solar nebula); the Sun's hydrogen-dominated composition matching Jupiter and Saturn as evidence of a shared reservoir; planetesimals gathering under mutual gravity to build planets through violent collisions; the heat gradient explaining rocky inner planets and ice-rich outer bodies; and flattened circumstellar disks observed around young stars as contemporary analogs of our own solar nebula. Facts synthesized into original prose.
